ak-dof-fire-resistant-vegetation-2005.name: Protect Your Home from Wildfire — Fire Resistant Vegetation and Landscaping
ak-dof-fire-resistant-vegetation-2005.publisher: Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Division of Forestry, Community Forestry Program
ak-dof-fire-resistant-vegetation-2005.scaleNotes: The 56 printed taxa in the source's Alaska firewise-landscape examples map to recommend with its placement-and-maintenance condition. Four genus examples under Characteristics of plants that ignite and burn readily map to avoid. Accepted-name reconciliation collapses the 60 entries to 58 evidence owners.
ak-dof-fire-resistant-vegetation-2005.notes: All printed scientific identities were retained at their printed rank. Source spelling damage and obsolete combinations were reconciled only through explicit corrections and exact GBIF matches; source spellings remain in the parser and evidence claims. The taxon-free "Ferns, native and non-native" row was held. The guide gives no test method or citations, so tier remains unset and lineage unknown. Official PDF SHA-256: 68afb4eedbffab6e049e7c771326c1e9bd7a4f071ab2a754d256178b0fc7755e.

al-afc-firewise-woodland-homes-2001.name: Firewise Landscaping for Woodland Homes
al-afc-firewise-woodland-homes-2001.scaleNotes: The booklet separates suggested trees, shrubs, and groundcovers from four fire-prone plants to avoid within 30 feet of the house. Suggested rows map to recommend and the explicit avoid rows map to avoid.
al-afc-firewise-woodland-homes-2001.notes: The five-page Alabama Forestry Commission PDF was recovered from its 2002-09-13 Wayback capture after disappearing from the live site in 2003. Thirty-one printed occurrences resolve to 27 exact GBIF owners; the repeated Acer genus row is represented once. Three rows are held rather than broadened: one schema-inexpressible form and two named cultivars. Printed errors corrected transparently for matching are Celtis occidentallis -> Celtis occidentalis, Llex -> Ilex, and Magnolia stellara -> Magnolia stellata. PDF SHA-256: 760c681c6083d0ff6342ff2d4aacd5015b76005fee8358c9ac25979a51f5c74f.

anaheim-2018.name: Recommended Acceptable Fire Resistive Plant Species
anaheim-2018.notes: Derives from older State of California agency lists (the CA agency tree rooted in the LA Arboretum program). Southern California climate context; corroborates flammability claims, never regional suitability for the PNW.

apsvic.name: Fire Resistant and Retardant Plants
apsvic.scaleNotes: Two classes: fire-resistant (52 plants that will not burn in the face of continued flame) and fire-retardant (92 plants that resist the first wave of a bushfire but may burn once dried out). Both classes map to recommend, with the class preserved verbatim on each row.
apsvic.notes: Member-experience curation from burnt properties plus a foliage flare-up test — closer to field observation than list-copying, and independent of the CFA lineage. Carries the Sweet Pittosporum delisting: previously fire-retardant, now noted as highly flammable once dried, agreeing with Tasmania's X-coded row.

ashland-best-practices.name: Best Practices for Fire Resistant Landscaping
ashland-best-practices.scaleNotes: Recommendations defer to PNW 590; the prohibited-species list (AMC 9.04.022, adopted by resolution) is original regulatory content with legal force.
ashland-best-practices.notes: Prohibited list rows are adoption/regulatory evidence; recommendation rows are PNW 590-derivative.

ashland-prohibited.name: Prohibited Flammable Plants (Ashland Municipal Code 9.04)
ashland-prohibited.publisher: City of Ashland, Oregon (Fire & Rescue / Weed Abatement)
ashland-prohibited.scaleNotes: A municipal prohibition list: the named trees, shrubs, and grasses may not be newly planted or allowed to propagate within 30 feet of any structure (AMC 9.04), with canopy- and shrub-spacing standards under AMC 18.3.10.100. Verdict map: prohibited = avoid. Starred taxa may receive dwarf or prostrate-variety exceptions with fire department approval.
ashland-prohibited.notes: Regulatory evidence, not a flammability measurement — an adopted ordinance that corroborates avoid verdicts. Assigned to the pnw590 tree conservatively: an Oregon ordinance in the PNW-guidance sphere has not been demonstrated independent of that lineage, and independence must be shown, never assumed and matters directly to the Oregon audience. Mostly genus-level rows (all pines, all junipers, all cedars), which attach to genus records and leave species-level lab evidence undisturbed.

bardon-2005.name: Firewise Landscaping in North Carolina (E05-44596)
bardon-2005.publisher: NC State University / NC Cooperative Extension + USFWS (Bardon, Van Druten)
bardon-2005.scaleNotes: Four-tier flammability rating (Low / Medium / High / Extreme) for ~200 North Carolina natives, by growth form with habitat columns. Verdict map: Low = recommend, Medium = mixed, High and Extreme = avoid.
bardon-2005.notes: The root of all NC ratings, including (near-certainly) the Plant Toolbox, whose signature four-value scale this document originated. National Fire Plan funded. Agency copy retired; town mirrors persist.

batista-2013-green-barriers-gtr245.name: Evaluation of the flammability of trees and shrubs used in green barriers in southern Brazil
batista-2013-green-barriers-gtr245.publisher: USDA Forest Service (Batista, Biondi, Tetto et al.; Universidade Federal do Paraná)
batista-2013-green-barriers-gtr245.scaleNotes: The paper applies Valette's 0-5 epiradiator flammability scale to live leaves and thin branches. Verdict map: 0-1 (non/low flammability) = recommend; 2-3 (moderately flammable/flammable) = mixed; 4-5 (highly/extremely flammable) = avoid.
batista-2013-green-barriers-gtr245.notes: Complete English full text and Table 2 are publicly hosted by the USDA Forest Service. All five exact species are represented. Batista, Biondi, Tetto, and Kovalsyki recur in the UFPR green-barrier program, so this and its Brazilian companion papers share one ufpr-cortinas-tree vote. Use of Valette's method alone does not merge this new dataset with Valette's INRA lineage.

batista-biondi-2009-ligustrum.name: Flammability evaluation of Ligustrum lucidum for potential use in fuelbreaks
batista-biondi-2009-ligustrum.publisher: Revista Brasileira de Ciências Agrárias (Batista & Biondi; UFPR)
batista-biondi-2009-ligustrum.scaleNotes: Verdicts follow the authors' explicit interpretation of replicated 1 m2 burn plots: Ligustrum lucidum = low flammability/recommend; Pinus taeda = high-flammability control/avoid. Rate of spread, flame height, and fire intensity remain in the evidence claims rather than being remapped.
batista-biondi-2009-ligustrum.notes: The complete CC-BY full text and result tables are publicly available. Both exact measured taxa are represented. Batista's UFPR laboratory, method program, and later-paper authorship connect this experiment to the ufpr-cortinas-tree, so it enriches that lineage without adding a vote.

behm-2004-florida-understory.name: Flammability of native understory species in pine flatwood and hardwood hammock ecosystems
behm-2004-florida-understory.publisher: International Journal of Wildland Fire (Behm, Duryea, Long, Zipperer)
behm-2004-florida-understory.scaleNotes: The paper rejects a single composite flammability index and instead names four taxa as the most flammable, one as the least flammable, and describes wax myrtle's measured characteristics as moderate. Verdict map: the named most-flammable group = avoid; the named least-flammable taxon = recommend; every other measured taxon = mixed. No threshold or score is inferred.
behm-2004-florida-understory.notes: Species-level fuel structure, biomass, moisture, volatile-solids, and energy measurements for ten unique taxa sampled as twelve ecosystem-by-species groups. The author-uploaded article is publicly readable in full. Behm, Long, and Zipperer overlap the later Long 2006 whole-plant study, so both papers remain one ufifas-srs-tree lineage vote.

canberra-plant-selector.name: Canberra Plant Selector — fire-retardant attribute
canberra-plant-selector.scaleNotes: The public selector exposes a Fire Retardant Yes/No filter and repeats the selected attribute on each result card. Only Yes rows map to recommend. No is absence of the positive selector attribute and is not converted to an avoid verdict.
canberra-plant-selector.notes: The live 2026-08-25 tool reports 259 total plants and 131 Fire Retardant: Yes plants, replacing the registry's stale estimate of 342. All 22 filtered result pages were captured at one request per second. Named cultivars were collapsed only where the printed label also states a species; genus-only hybrid/cultivar labels, two authorless homonyms, an unrepresentable subspecies row, and a variety collapsed by GBIF were held. Of 131 printed Yes rows, 122 exact GBIF owners are represented (72 existing records enriched and 50 records created); nine rows are retained in the ledger as held.

cflo-2023-caatinga-fire-behavior.name: Comportamento do fogo em espécies nativas da Caatinga na região geográfica imediata de Patos-PB
cflo-2023-caatinga-fire-behavior.publisher: Ciência Florestal, Universidade Federal de Santa Maria
cflo-2023-caatinga-fire-behavior.scaleNotes: Ten species were compared in three replicated outdoor 1 m² burns. Tables 6-9 report ignition attempts/time, flame height, combustibility index, spread rate, fire intensity, and severity. Only Cnidoscolus quercifolius and Aristida adscensionis receive explicit overall flammability conclusions.
cflo-2023-caatinga-fire-behavior.notes: Leaves and branches no more than 0.7 cm in diameter were air-dried for 30 days; each treatment used 9 kg of fuel. Cnidoscolus quercifolius did not sustain flame spread, so it is absent from the later metric tables and its fire intensity is described as zero. PDF SHA-256: e982b13fcd9d796607f66d7b1cec059e2bcd8ac621296b1506612f4c67579c75.

corbett-safer-gardens-2021.name: Safer Gardens: Plant Flammability & Planning for Fire
corbett-safer-gardens-2021.scaleNotes: The book synthesizes low, moderate, and high plant flammability findings, preserving conflicts among primary studies. The public 56-page sample omits Chapter 10's Plant Flammability Table. Only explicit taxon-level findings in the public sample and author website were admitted: low = recommend, high = avoid, and conditional or seasonally conflicting findings = mixed.
corbett-safer-gardens-2021.notes: Eleven exact public findings were ingested. The website publishes a 500-plus plant name index, but names alone are not ratings and were not converted to evidence. The omitted full table remains a documented access gap. Captures: home HTML SHA-256 796bcc99d5ba13c5ab969be6d2d166740fd1099c48cf262105a31f19114daabf; plants-page HTML SHA-256 55f04e58431bc64e98e5e96825cbdbb30acd7b07f029879df8ab32dcf4c3c04e; public sample PDF SHA-256 581815b6ffd6a18c89ff33bdb55e296d3c98261060709810d003efcdc7304334.

csiro-bushfire-best-practice-landscaping.name: Bushfire Best Practice Guide — Landscaping
csiro-bushfire-best-practice-landscaping.scaleNotes: The guide is almost entirely design-, maintenance-, and trait-based. Its one explicit taxon-level suitability statement names Grevillea at genus rank; that statement maps to recommend. Generic advice to choose low-flammability species was not converted into taxon evidence.
csiro-bushfire-best-practice-landscaping.notes: One exact GBIF genus owner was created from the shrubs-page image caption. The landing page and all 12 landscaping child pages were captured and read; the remaining pages name plant forms and materials, not taxa. Main-page HTML SHA-256 f95ab0ddf5ec4b174c79476a91556cb6acb350a3be968cbaf771808aa1dea28c; shrubs-page HTML SHA-256 4831b0e8cc874f3108f1969a31c2eb38fddcae0bcd2b1ee356aa6136e539c4c5.

csu-6305.name: Ignition-Resistant Landscape Plants (Fact Sheet 6.305)
csu-6305.publisher: Colorado State University Extension / Colorado State Forest Service (Wildfire Mitigation Series)
csu-6305.scaleNotes: 114 ignition-resistant plants scored 7.5-10 on the 0-10 ignitability scale, with the fact sheet's own doctrine that only plants scoring 8, 9, or 10 belong in defensible-space zones 1 and 2. Verdict map: 8-10 = recommend, 7.5 = mixed (below the source's own zone-1-2 bar). The sheet credits "the Idaho materials" as the basis of the scoring, so rows whose scores duplicate the Idaho Firewise master database resolve to that root.
csu-6305.notes: The 2025 revision replaces the unscored FireWise Plant Materials lists of the 2001-2010 editions (Wayback captures archived for edition-diffing). A recommend-side list only; it condemns nothing. Exact replay audited 2026-08-25: all 114 rows resolve to existing GBIF owners, using nine documented exact corrections. Seventy-eight score-identical rows resolve to Idaho via original; 36 rows remain CSU-original. The hardened parser creates no records and every row carries full table placement and lineage.

dehane-2017-cork-oak-companions.name: Flammability of some companion species in cork oak forests
dehane-2017-cork-oak-companions.publisher: Annals of Forest Science (Dehane, Hernando, Guijarro & Madrigal)
dehane-2017-cork-oak-companions.scaleNotes: K-means classifications of fresh and oven-dried fuels differ. The paper's abstract explicitly identifies Calicotome spinosa, Tetraclinis articulata, Juniperus oxycedrus, and Pinus halepensis as highly flammable. Verdict map: this explicit overall high group = avoid; all other measured taxa = mixed. No recommend verdict is inferred from a favorable fresh-only cluster.
dehane-2017-cork-oak-companions.notes: The complete article is publicly archived in HAL. All ten exact species are represented. Fresh twigs with foliage and paired oven-dried samples were tested by mass-loss calorimeter. Hernando, Guijarro, and Madrigal place this in the INIA Madrid fire-lab program already represented by Ganteaume; the Algerian samples are new data but share one inia-madrid-tree vote.

della-rocca-2015-cypress-lab.name: Possible land management uses of common cypress to reduce wildfire initiation risk: a laboratory study
della-rocca-2015-cypress-lab.publisher: Elsevier / Journal of Environmental Management (IPSP-CNR and INIA-CIFOR)
della-rocca-2015-cypress-lab.scaleNotes: Component-level study of Cupressus sempervirens var. horizontalis live crown and dead litter. The authors report relative resistance to ignition and low crown/litter ignitability, while requiring multiple methods to characterize sustainability, combustibility, and consumability. Both rows map to mixed; no overall low-flammability class is inferred.
della-rocca-2015-cypress-lab.notes: Tier 1 bench-scale laboratory study using mass-loss calorimetry, epiradiator, and oxygen bomb methods. The selected-variety cypress-barrier application is framed as a promising complementary tool needing further study. Evidence remains variety-, part-, moisture-, and placement-specific and does not roll up to the species or genus.

dibble-2007-northeastern-invasives.name: Combustion characteristics of north-eastern USA vegetation tested in the cone calorimeter
dibble-2007-northeastern-invasives.publisher: International Journal of Wildland Fire (Dibble, White, Lebow)
dibble-2007-northeastern-invasives.scaleNotes: The paper reports several cone-calorimeter measurements and warns that their rankings are not interchangeable. Verdicts therefore use only the abstract's author-named effective-heat-of-combustion extremes: taxa named high = avoid; taxa named low = recommend; every other measured taxon = mixed. This is a map of the conditioned foliage-and-twig result, not a whole-plant claim.
dibble-2007-northeastern-invasives.notes: Public full text is hosted by the USDA Forest Service. Thirty-six identified vascular taxa are represented. Vitis sp. and Cynanchum cf. louiseae are excluded because the paper does not provide an exact species identification; three bryophytes and one lichen are excluded because the current directory schema has no defensible nonvascular plant form. Dibble and White overlap the Forest Products Laboratory cone-calorimeter program represented by White et al. 2002 and Weise et al. 2005, so this is one usfs-fpl-cone-tree vote.

dovetail-ne-minnesota.name: Landscaping for Wildfire Defensible Space in Northeastern Minnesota (Firewise)
dovetail-ne-minnesota.publisher: Dovetail Partners (Ely, MN; supported by The Nature Conservancy / USDA Forest Service PERFACT agreement)
dovetail-ne-minnesota.scaleNotes: Table 2 rates 38 wildfire-resistant, non-invasive plants low or moderate flammability using the UF/IFAS Circular 1453 methodology (Behm, Long, Monroe, Randall, Zipperer, Hermansen-Baez 2004), with the document's own placement mapping — low-flammability plants may be planted 3 to 30 feet from a building, moderate ones beyond 30 feet. Verdict map: low = recommend, moderate = mixed.
dovetail-ne-minnesota.notes: The only rated Minnesota list; a clean application of the Florida flammability key to northeastern Minnesota natives, with growing-condition columns (form, soil moisture, sun, hardiness zones). The document's boreal-tree flammability table (Table 1) is attributed to Manitoba's FireSmart program and is not part of this source's own ratings.

fdacs-south-florida-firewise-guide.name: Landscaping to Reduce Wildfire Risk: South Florida Edition
fdacs-south-florida-firewise-guide.scaleNotes: Narrative hazard callouts rather than a ranked plant table. The guide calls five named invasive plants extremely flammable, flags grape vine as a fire concern, calls palmetto highly combustible, and describes condition-dependent fire spread on cabbage palm.
fdacs-south-florida-firewise-guide.notes: Written and designed for the Florida Forest Service by Melissa Yunas and Victor Hill. The guide links Firewise and University of Florida resources but gives no claim-level provenance or rating method, so its evidence lineage remains unknown. The eight represented owners preserve only taxonomic precision supported by the printed common or genus names. Official PDF SHA-256: 883a3538a62612580f8e4758df34283d91d11b04b5260702138c3c0edf316a89.

fenz-low-flammability.name: Low Flammability Plants directory
fenz-low-flammability.publisher: Fire and Emergency New Zealand (plant flammability testing at Lincoln University)
fenz-low-flammability.scaleNotes: Seven-level flammability classification (Very low / Low / Low-moderate / Moderate / Moderate-high / High / Very high) across 402 species, grounded in shoot-flammability testing at Lincoln University (the Curran-group "plant barbecue" program). Verdict map: very low, low, and low-moderate = recommend (the directory calls low and low-moderate species ideal for planting); moderate and moderate-high = mixed; high and very high = avoid. A separate list of twelve high-flammability environmental weeds (2024 Department of Conservation list) maps to avoid.
fenz-low-flammability.notes: The deepest lab-derived official plant flammability directory anywhere, and the corpus's first Southern Hemisphere lab chain. Website content is CC-BY-NC-ND, so only uncopyrightable facts are extracted — species names, classifications, and poisonous/weed flags — with attribution in text. Accessed via FENZ's checkitsalright.nz property; origin column is NZ-relative.

fernandes-2020-selective-shrub-mgmt.name: Selective Shrub Management to Preserve Mediterranean Forests and Reduce the Risk of Fire
fernandes-2020-selective-shrub-mgmt.publisher: MDPI Fire / University of Évora and Instituto Politécnico de Viana do Castelo
fernandes-2020-selective-shrub-mgmt.scaleNotes: Table 2 marks 16 native genera Control in mainland Portugal fuel-management bands. Control maps to avoid only within that placement. The 18 Preserve genera are not mapped to recommend because the decision also incorporates succession, conservation value, and protected status.
fernandes-2020-selective-shrub-mgmt.notes: Perspective grounded in phytosociology, literature synthesis, and the authors' 2017 post-fire observation. Fine-textured heliophilous shrubs are prioritized for selective control. The stable registry slug predates source inspection; the actual authors are Raposo, Pinto Gomes, and Nunes, not Fernandes.

firesafe-marin.name: Fire-Resistant Plants Common to Marin County
firesafe-marin.scaleNotes: The publication separates named fire-resistant plants from a shorter fire-prone list. It also identifies plants suitable for hedges. Fire Safe Marin says placement, spacing, irrigation, and removal of dead material remain necessary; it does not describe an experimental rating method.
firesafe-marin.notes: The source remains tierless because its selection lineage is only partly documented. Its rows publish Marin's curation and conflicts without creating independent Tier 1 support in the derived rating.

firesmart-bc.name: FireSmart BC Plant Program — fire-resistant plant chart
firesmart-bc.scaleNotes: Binary FireSmart-approved chart of 290 plants across eight growth-form categories, each with a Home Ignition Zone suitability (intermediate 10-30 m / extended 30-100 m / extended and beyond) or a needs-more-research flag. Verdict map: approved = recommend.
firesmart-bc.notes: Tier 2 compiled corroboration: FireSmart BC's chart substantially republishes the PNW-590 species set for BC, so rows landing on records that already carry pnw-590 evidence resolve to that root and add no independence. Zone suitability is preserved as placement guidance; needs-more-research flags travel as claims.

firewise-arkansas-plant-guide.name: FireWise Plants offer colorful choices for Fire Safe Gardens
firewise-arkansas-plant-guide.scaleNotes: The page presents its 19-row table as a short representation of Firewise trees, shrubs, and groundcovers homeowners can choose. Every table row maps to recommend. Its unscientific generic avoid examples are held separately.
firewise-arkansas-plant-guide.notes: Nineteen exact GBIF species owners were admitted from the visually audited table. Printed Juglans cincerea and Rhus copallinum errors were corrected transparently to Juglans cinerea and Rhus copallina. The generic warning to avoid pine, cedar, and juniper was not converted because it supplies no scientific names and cedar is taxonomically ambiguous. PDF SHA-256: 9b2a00c8c2cbd815c797e67d0d34e0d5207a53e3088e4e97af35036ba1999a20.

firewise-black-hills-sd-plantlist.name: Firewise Plant Material for the Black Hills
firewise-black-hills-sd-plantlist.scaleNotes: The single-page list describes every table row as a fire-resistive plant that can be used in landscaping. Each exact taxon row maps to recommend; the page provides no comparative score or avoid category.
firewise-black-hills-sd-plantlist.notes: Forty-eight printed rows were visually audited. Forty-seven exact GBIF genus or species owners are represented and one unranked infraspecific chokecherry label is held rather than broadened. Nine obvious printed misspellings are preserved in verdictRaw and corrected transparently for matching. PDF SHA-256: 6e2b8c1d6e58801cf206de42e90f1bbd95cb496422bb0fe45d21dd5c7e910f9e.

firewise-uk-dorset-leaflet-2024.name: Protecting your home from wildfire — plants and tips that can reduce your risk
firewise-uk-dorset-leaflet-2024.publisher: Dorset Heaths Partnership / Firewise UK / University of Exeter wildFIRE Lab
firewise-uk-dorset-leaflet-2024.scaleNotes: University of Exeter wildFIRE Lab testing is published as green, amber, and red classes. Verdict map: green = recommend; amber = mixed; red = avoid. The leaflet defines red dry material as capable of flames over 2.5 m.
firewise-uk-dorset-leaflet-2024.notes: The two-page public leaflet and its visual class columns were verified. Eleven unambiguously identified species/cultivars were ingested. Seventeen entries labelled only by a genus or ambiguous common name were excluded rather than assigned a taxon. This is one exeter-wildfire-tree lab program vote.

fitzgerald-waldo-2002-osu-frn6.name: Fire-Resistant Plants for Oregon Home Landscapes
fitzgerald-waldo-2002-osu-frn6.scaleNotes: Binary inclusion in Fire-Resistant Plant Materials for Oregon, organized into groundcovers, perennials, broadleaf evergreen shrubs, deciduous shrubs, evergreen trees, and deciduous trees. A few rows carry Central, Eastern, Southern, or Western Oregon placement codes.
fitzgerald-waldo-2002-osu-frn6.notes: Direct precursor of joint PNW 590 and therefore assigned the same lineage rather than an independent vote. The guide says most listed plants require some irrigation during dry summers and that even fire-resistant plants can burn if not maintained in a healthy condition. Capture SHA-256: 3e719b3edaf3502e42f384d7972b8c79511aa85cba25d7b3234fd60fac2df954.

flamits.name: FLAMITS: FLAMmability plant traiTS database
flamits.scaleNotes: FLAMITS stores 19,972 numeric observations across 40 harmonized variables and five flammability dimensions. Values retain the published variable name, experimental context, and primary-study identifier. They are represented as non-voting measurements because the database does not impose one directional threshold across unlike variables, devices, plant parts, or fuel conditions.
flamits.notes: CC0 dataset compiled from 295 primary flammability studies. Each evidence row cites both the Dryad dataset and its original source_ID; the complete primary citations are preserved in flamits-sources.csv. Of 19,972 published rows, 19,500 are admitted on 1,736 exact accepted identities. The hold ledger keeps 164 rows whose source_ID is absent from the supplied reference table and 308 rows whose taxon cannot be represented by an exact genus/species identity. Dataset version 9 data-file SHA-256: 8c876f4550ac032af98071d018dd2f76fbc96a21d1f26293ca4065537080f39c.

fps-eastern-us.name: Eastern United States Fire Performance Plant Selector
fps-eastern-us.publisher: USDA Forest Service Northeastern Area S&PF + state Firewise programs (WV, OH, PA, DE, DC, MD, NJ)
fps-eastern-us.scaleNotes: Firewise Rating 1-4: Firewise (1), Moderately Firewise (2), At Risk (3), Not Firewise (4). Landscape Zones LZ1-4 give the program's own placement.
fps-eastern-us.notes: Ratings assigned by Larry Steward (OSU-ATI) using the UF Circular 1453 flammability key modified for northeastern dormancy; concept by Bob Hannah (WV Division of Forestry). The program's website is dead; FireApproved's Wayback recovery (541 of 541 species, cross-validated against the 2014 master table) is the only surviving copy of the dataset. Exact-identity audit 2026-08-25: 539 rows represented by 533 evidence owners, including two not-rated source anomalies; two cultivar-group rows are taxonomy-held.

france-old-debroussaillement.name: Débroussaillement — Le Guide Complet : conseils et règlementation
france-old-debroussaillement.publisher: Prévention Incendies de Forêt / Entente Valabre
france-old-debroussaillement.scaleNotes: The page gives structural legal-clearing guidance rather than a national species scale. One non-statutory plant-level warning says that conifer hedges of the cypress type are the most combustible; that warning maps to avoid at genus rank and remains conditioned on hedge form and accumulated dead/resinous material.
france-old-debroussaillement.notes: Only the explicit Cupressus genus warning was admitted. No national French recommended or prohibited species list was inferred. The page was published 2016-12-13 and reports modification on 2025-06-20 in its embedded metadata. HTML capture SHA-256: 2d445bbee3ab32bd8b66a5213bf24425e29b729ca6969d750f627d971f44f2a2.

fremont-county-wy-firewise-list.name: Fremont County Firewise Plant List
fremont-county-wy-firewise-list.scaleNotes: The page presents every row in its Ground Covers, Shrubs, and Large Shrubs and Trees sections as a Firewise plant. Listed taxa map to recommend. The page provides no comparative classes or adverse list.
fremont-county-wy-firewise-list.notes: The page describes Firewise plants as generally low-growing, low-debris, and relatively moist, but gives no methodology or source attribution. It remains Tier 2 with unknown lineage. Thirteen explicitly genus-level entries remain genus records; common names were not widened to inferred species. Obvious typographical errors in scientific names were reconciled only to exact GBIF matches and the printed spellings remain in verdictRaw. Raw HTML SHA-256: 895416d7024cfbcb4f5f475d1b8f3b81a0a3999b249dfd3152a75e2bd1f30a88.

ganteaume-2013-provence-ornamental-hedge.name: Flammability of some ornamental species in wildland-urban interfaces in southeastern France
ganteaume-2013-provence-ornamental-hedge.publisher: Environmental Management (Ganteaume, Jappiot, Lampin, Guijarro, Hernando)
ganteaume-2013-provence-ornamental-hedge.scaleNotes: The hierarchical analysis assigns poorly flammable, not very flammable, moderately flammable, highly flammable, and extremely flammable clusters. Verdict map: poorly/not very = recommend; moderately = mixed; highly/extremely = avoid. For Cupressus sempervirens the row follows the paper's overall conclusion: live leaves were not very flammable, but its accumulated dead leaves were extremely flammable and the authors say the species should be avoided near houses.
ganteaume-2013-provence-ornamental-hedge.notes: Public author-produced full text is archived by HAL. Six exact species are represented; Phyllostachys sp. is excluded because the paper identifies it only to genus. Guijarro and Hernando overlap the INIA Madrid fire-lab papers, so this source conservatively shares the inia-madrid-tree vote. It uses Valette's published epiradiator protocol and scale, but has different authors and a new ornamental dataset, so protocol reuse alone does not merge it with Valette 1990.

gencat-franges-perimetrals.name: Les franges perimetrals de protecció contra els incendis forestals
gencat-franges-perimetrals.scaleNotes: The page 4 species-selection panel instructs managers to maintain first the less-flammable species and to remove first the more-flammable species. gonzalez-2022-laguna-blanca-wui.name: Fire hazard assessment at different scales in the WUI of semiarid northern Patagonia

gonzalez-2022-laguna-blanca-wui.scaleNotes: The abstract and Discussion explicitly name the most-flammable species after considering leaf and plant variables. Verdict map: author-named most-flammable taxa measured in this paper = avoid; all other taxa measured in this paper = mixed. No low direction is inferred from a single favorable component.
gonzalez-2022-laguna-blanca-wui.notes: Complete CC-BY full text is openly published by Frontiers. Eight exact taxa were newly sampled; Mulinum spinosum is excluded because this article imports its data from Blackhall and Raffaele 2019. Three of the newly measured taxa belong to the paper's four-member most-flammable group. This is a new Gonzalez/Ghermandi Laguna Blanca dataset; citation or import of one Blackhall result does not merge the eight new measurements with the earlier paper.

guerrero-2020-valparaiso-thermo.name: Thermo- and physicochemical properties of native and exotic forest species of Valparaíso
guerrero-2020-valparaiso-thermo.publisher: International Journal of Wildland Fire (Guerrero et al.; UTFSM)

gva-valencia.name: Jardinería de baja inflamabilidad para las zonas de interfaz urbano-forestal
gva-valencia.scaleNotes: A recommended-species table for wildland-urban-interface gardens (92 entries across hedges, climbers, trees, shrubs, and beds, in native and garden columns) plus a flammable-species warning naming pines, heaths, cypresses, esparto, and rosemary. Verdict map: recommended = recommend, named-flammable = avoid. Thymus vulgaris appears on both sides and is recorded as mixed with the tension preserved.
gva-valencia.notes: The corpus's first Spanish-language source under the all-English extraction policy (English claims, Spanish claimOriginal). Its rosemary condemnation corroborates the INRA laboratory notes; its cypress caution is about dry-material accumulation, echoing the CypFire condition-not-species finding already documented in the source survey.

harrison-2002-rangelands-kochia-fires.name: Forage Kochia Helps Fight Range Fires
harrison-2002-rangelands-kochia-fires.scaleNotes: Table 1 contains 11 rows for species frequently used in greenstrips; its dual-species crested-wheatgrass row yields 12 taxon identities. Listed = recommend only within the recorded semiarid greenstrip placement. Eleven identities fit the current schema; the western-yarrow subspecies is held out because subspecies rank is unavailable.
harrison-2002-rangelands-kochia-fires.notes: Tier 1 expert synthesis based on reviewed reports, field observations, and telephone interviews. The source explicitly says published peer-reviewed fire-suppression findings were unavailable and asks for more quantitative research. Its controlled-burn and wildfire figures are specific to forage kochia; companion Table 1 species are not recast as individually tested. Same greenstrip-tree lineage as the underlying BLM, USFS, UNR, and NRCS work.

henaoui-cistus-tlemcen.name: The fire risk of the plant groupings with Cistus in the area of Tlemcen (Western Algeria)
henaoui-cistus-tlemcen.scaleNotes: Table 1 classifies fresh-material ignition delay as note 3 / high flammability at 65 seconds or less, note 2 / moderate above 65 and below 130 seconds, and note 1 / low at 130 seconds or more.
henaoui-cistus-tlemcen.notes: The authors tested three fresh 10 g samples for each of 38 species with an infrared burner at 850 °C during April-May 2013. The separate narrative aside naming four non-flammable plants is not ingested because those taxa are absent from the stated 38-species experimental set and Table 1. idaho-firewise-master-db.name: Fire Resistance of Plants Master Database
idaho-firewise-master-db.publisher: Idaho Firewise (BLM + College of Western Idaho + Idaho Botanical Garden)
idaho-firewise-master-db.scaleNotes: 0-10 fire-resistance score mapped by the source to minimum planting distance (10 = acceptable at 10 ft ... 1 = keep 100+ ft away). Verdict thresholds follow CSU's published usage of this scale: 8-10 recommend, 4-7 mixed, 0-3 avoid.
idaho-firewise-master-db.notes: The largest scored US dataset (400+ species and cultivars). Cooperative scoring program; its methodology was adopted by CSU/CSFS in 2025.

isees-2021-judean-hills.name: השרפה בהרי יהודה – 2021: ניתוח, תובנות והמלצות
isees-2021-judean-hills.scaleNotes: The recommendations call for reducing pine presence in forest fire-buffer strips and interrupting dense pine continuity, mapped to avoid at Pinus genus rank with its placement condition. Five exact species are offered as less-flammable alternatives to pines in public-use forest areas, mapped to recommend.
isees-2021-judean-hills.notes: Six exact GBIF owners are admitted: one Pinus genus row and five species rows. The article's printed Ceratonia silique typo is preserved in verdictRaw and transparently corrected to Ceratonia siliqua for matching. jaureguiberry-2011-device-34spp.name: Device for the standard measurement of shoot flammability in the field
jaureguiberry-2011-device-34spp.publisher: Austral Ecology / IMBIV-CONICET and Universidad Nacional de Córdoba
jaureguiberry-2011-device-34spp.scaleNotes: Appendix S5 publishes continuous means for MT, BL, BT, BR, BB interval, and the authors' compound FL index for 34 samples. FL runs from 0 toward roughly 3, but the paper defines no directional taxon classes or cutoffs. All rows are retained as not-rated measurements.
jaureguiberry-2011-device-34spp.notes: Six fresh field samples per taxon were preheated for two minutes at 150 °C and ignited for 10 seconds. Thirty-four sample rows resolve to 33 exact GBIF identities because Celtis ehrenbergiana was deliberately measured as both tree and shrub morphotypes. The Appendix S2 spelling Pappophorum explicitly corrects S5's Papophorum typo.

king-county-puget-sound-2011.name: Firewise Plants for the Puget Sound Basin
king-county-puget-sound-2011.scaleNotes: Binary recommendation by presence in the source's Trees, Shrubs, Perennials, or Groundcovers tables under the heading Fire-resistant Landscape Plants.
king-county-puget-sound-2011.notes: Native-first King County curation for the Puget Sound Basin. Its only named resources are the Washington Native Plant Society and Pojar & MacKinnon's Plants of the Pacific Northwest Coast; it does not cite PNW 590.

kkl-2024-fire-prevention-compendium.name: מסמך מאגד הנחיות למניעת שרפות ולשיקום יער לאחר שרפות
kkl-2024-fire-prevention-compendium.scaleNotes: The guide repeatedly prioritizes cypress trees over conifers when selecting retained trees in settlement and forest fire-buffer strips. This operational genus-level preference maps to recommend. Broad structural prescriptions and unnamed woodland, broadleaf, conifer, and vegetation classes are not mapped.
kkl-2024-fire-prevention-compendium.notes: One exact Cupressus genus row is admitted from pages 4, 6, and 7. The guide contains no species table or named cypress species, so the evidence stays at genus rank. PDF SHA-256: 6115cbf79c7b18dc0201f80c8d9df79d0879cb61a277aec1173de2322bf40c0e.

kovalsyki-2016-pfb-cortinas.name: Flammability of tree species for use in fuelbreaks in forest-fire prevention
kovalsyki-2016-pfb-cortinas.publisher: Pesquisa Florestal Brasileira (Kovalsyki, Takashina, Tres, Tetto & Batista; UFPR)
kovalsyki-2016-pfb-cortinas.scaleNotes: Table 4 reports Valette's 0-5 flammability value (VI) separately from the combustion-intensity index (IC). Verdicts use VI only: 0-1 (non/poorly flammable) = recommend; 2-3 (moderately flammable/flammable) = mixed; 4-5 (highly/extremely flammable) = avoid. IC is retained only as a measurement.
kovalsyki-2016-pfb-cortinas.notes: Complete Portuguese full text, English abstract, and species Tables 3-4 are openly published by Embrapa. Four candidate species and the Pinus taeda control are represented. Batista, Tetto, Kovalsyki, and Tres overlap the 2013 UFPR experiment, so the papers share one ufpr-cortinas-tree vote. The registry's earlier summary confused combustion intensity with flammability; Table 4 is the controlling result.

la-arboretum-fire-retardant-hillside-197.name: Fire-Retardant Plants for Brush Fire Prevention in Hillside Residential Areas
la-arboretum-fire-retardant-hillside-197.scaleNotes: Table 1 recommends 30 low-growing shrubs and herbaceous perennials in four fire-retardance categories based on leaf moisture capacity: Category 1, greatest (90-95%); Category 2, high (80-95%); Category 3, medium-high (70-80%); and Category 4, least among the recommended set (60-70%).
la-arboretum-fire-retardant-hillside-197.notes: The Arboretum's official archive links to the Missouri Botanical Garden scan of LASCA Leaves. The authors condition the recommendations on watering through the dry season and maintenance that removes accumulated litter. Internet Archive item mobot31753002430269; capture SHA-256: 8621cb11620bc2ad508532319b9cc009ae57ad8909f4de6ab74e71e3874d7c35.

long-2006-srs.name: Quantifying and ranking the flammability of ornamental shrubs in the southern United States
long-2006-srs.publisher: USDA Forest Service Southern Research Station + NIST (Long, Behm, Zipperer, Hermansen, Maranghides, Mell)
long-2006-srs.scaleNotes: Whole-plant burns with large-scale calorimetry at NIST BFRL; cluster analysis produced 22 low / 8 moderate / 4 high flammability among 34 ornamental shrubs. Verdict map: low = recommend, moderate = mixed, high = avoid.
long-2006-srs.notes: The most direct US lab ranking of ornamental shrubs; the evidence base behind UF/IFAS FOR272. Cite as "burns conducted at NIST BFRL" — no standalone NIST report exists.

lsu-hammond.name: Firewise Landscaping (Hammond Research Station)
lsu-hammond.scaleNotes: A prose list of 31 ornamentals "recommended for firewise landscaping" in Louisiana, mostly at genus level. Verdict map: listed = recommend. Tier is deliberately omitted — no methodology is cited, so rows are corroboration only and can never move a rating on their own.
lsu-hammond.notes: Louisiana's only named-species list. Same structural treatment as the NC Plant Toolbox: an undocumented assignment corroborates but does not promote.

lubin-shelly-1997-ucfpl-compilation.name: Defensible Space Landscaping in the Urban/Wildland Interface: A Compilation of Fire Performance Ratings of Residential Landscape Plants
lubin-shelly-1997-ucfpl-compilation.publisher: University of California Forest Products Laboratory
lubin-shelly-1997-ucfpl-compilation.scaleNotes: The report compiles more than 25 earlier lists. Chapter 2 requires at least three favorable references, Chapter 3 requires at least three unfavorable references, and Chapter 4 identifies conflicting source recommendations. These map to recommend, avoid, and mixed. The report says the underlying lists often lack scientific basis and use undefined terms.
lubin-shelly-1997-ucfpl-compilation.notes: Tier 2 compilation and the citation root behind several later California list wrappers. The recovered report is the evidence source. A preserved UCFPL column in the 2024 Living With Fire workbook is used only as a transcription aid for the report's F/U/C marker and reference count; it is not treated as another evidence lineage. Conservative exact reconciliation yields 130 evidence owners (83 favorable, 31 conflicting, 16 unfavorable), with 31 compound or non-exact taxonomy rows held.

lucas-2019-biobr-ornamentais.name: Flammability of urban ornamental species for use in green firebreaks
lucas-2019-biobr-ornamentais.publisher: Biodiversidade Brasileira (Lucas, Kovalsyki, Jacobs, Tetto & Batista; UFPR)
lucas-2019-biobr-ornamentais.scaleNotes: Both taxa are explicitly classified weakly flammable based on ignition frequency and time, despite high combustion intensity. Verdict map: author-classified weakly flammable = recommend. Component measurements and the high-intensity caveat are retained in each evidence row.
lucas-2019-biobr-ornamentais.notes: The complete one-page Portuguese conference paper is openly published and contains species-level methods and results. The 2020 English item repeats the same authors, taxa, sample counts, and values and is an edition/translation, not an independent source. Shared UFPR authors and epiradiator program place both rows in the existing ufpr-cortinas-tree.

lwf-plant-list-generator.name: Living With Fire Plant List Generator (2024-03-05 workbook)
lwf-plant-list-generator.publisher: Living With Fire (Charisse Sydoriak, compiler; Ashland OR)
lwf-plant-list-generator.scaleNotes: Aggregator with per-species attribution to original sources; used as a carrier (via) for rows whose originals are registered, never as its own verdict.
lwf-plant-list-generator.notes: 1,342-plant workbook recovered 2026-08-23 after the site's own download link died. Preserves per-species citations to the dead Fire Performance Plant Selector (231 rows) and the Idaho Master Database (377 rows). Audited 2026-08-25 as a carrier only: 47 missing root-source rows were recovered on 47 owners (29 existing and 18 new), while 184 candidate channels already had direct primary evidence and were not duplicated. The audit ledger records 93 attribution-only markers and every taxonomy, exact-match, value, or form hold.

macalister-2025-sajb-cape-town.name: Time to extinguish the exotic flame: Lessons from the 2021 Cape Town fire
macalister-2025-sajb-cape-town.publisher: South African Journal of Botany / University of Cape Town
macalister-2025-sajb-cape-town.region: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa
macalister-2025-sajb-cape-town.scaleNotes: Forty-two taxa were assessed for fresh- and dry-leaf ignitibility and sustainability plus combustibility. Twenty leaves were collected from each of five biological replicates per taxon; ten leaves were used for fresh tests and ten for dry tests after trait measurement.
macalister-2025-sajb-cape-town.notes: Laboratory means were recomputed from the official UCT raw-data workbook. Published Table 1 supplies identities and 2021 burn observations where the deposited workbook uses shorthand or contains typographical discrepancies. Native/exotic group differences are not converted into species verdicts. The abstract and methods state 22 native and 20 exotic taxa, while the published Table 1 labels and deposited workbook count 23 native and 19 exotic; the row-level labels are preserved without resolving that conflict. Phoenix canariensis and Pinus pinea receive avoid evidence only because the authors explicitly describe the former as a great danger during fire events and the latter as a wildfire hazard. Workbook SHA-256: 7f9ed8308007a35e522937252ed8fd84995b4c36ad2bfbe0d0604086aed3f46a.

madrigal-2013-bench-scale-live-fuels.name: A new bench-scale methodology for evaluating the flammability of live forest fuels
madrigal-2013-bench-scale-live-fuels.publisher: SAGE / Journal of Fire Sciences (INIA-CIFOR Forest Fire Laboratory)
madrigal-2013-bench-scale-live-fuels.scaleNotes: Table 1 reports five continuous variables for four live-fuel taxa at similar moisture content and 50 kW/m²: TTI, PHRR, AEHC, MLR, and THR. The authors publish no overall taxon class or composite rank. Rows are therefore direct laboratory evidence with verdict not-rated; all five means and repeatability standard deviations remain in claims.
madrigal-2013-bench-scale-live-fuels.notes: Tier 1 bench-scale study from the INIA-CIFOR laboratory. Component directions conflict, so deriving a recommend/avoid verdict would invent a weighting rule. Pinus pinaster uses live needles; the understory shrubs use leaves and fine twigs under 1 cm. Same inia-madrid-tree lineage as the earlier Spanish laboratory program.

maire-1962-landscape-to-prevent-fire.name: Landscape for Fire Protection
maire-1962-landscape-to-prevent-fire.publisher: University of California Agricultural Extension Service
maire-1962-landscape-to-prevent-fire.scaleNotes: The Plants for Fire Protection section gives a single conditioned recommendation set, organized as ground covers, shrubs, and trees. It describes these as examples for irrigated hillsides and repeatedly conditions performance on pruning, watering, and removing litter.
maire-1962-landscape-to-prevent-fire.notes: This 1968 AXT-254 edition replaces the physical-only 1962 AXT-64 Landscape to Prevent Fire. HathiTrust permits page-at-a-time viewing but instructed against saving or redistributing the scan; the repository therefore stores retrieval metadata rather than scan bytes. Four headings remain held because they identify a cultivar/form, a broad iceplant group, or an OCR spelling that does not exact-match GBIF.

mdfs-firewise-landscaping-plants.name: Firewise Landscaping Plants for Maryland
mdfs-firewise-landscaping-plants.publisher: Maryland Department of Natural Resources Forest Service
mdfs-firewise-landscaping-plants.scaleNotes: One affirmative list: every plant table row is described as relatively resistant to fire and as exhibiting stronger resistance to ignition by wildfires. The source publishes no comparative rating scale or row-level method.
mdfs-firewise-landscaping-plants.notes: Maryland is the canonical master of the Maryland/New Jersey/West Virginia template family; the state derivatives do not add independent votes. All 180 printed plant rows are preserved in an extracted row ledger. One exact botanical-form row is held because the plant schema cannot represent FORM rank; broadening it to the species would be dishonest. Mulch ignitability is outside the plant-evidence scope. PDF SHA-256: b349c0d9e454c1d5fa802f359b523a1f7b5f4da1da83a6b0274caff54234da14.

molina-2017-ignition-index.name: The ignition index based on flammability of vegetation improves planning in the WUI
molina-2017-ignition-index.publisher: Landscape and Urban Planning (Molina, Martín, Rodríguez y Silva & Herrera)
molina-2017-ignition-index.scaleNotes: Table 2 applies Valette classes 0-5. Verdict map: 0-1 = recommend, 2-3 = mixed, 4-5 = avoid. This paper's observed range is 2-5, so it supplies no recommend rows. Moisture, time to ignition, and flame duration are preserved.
molina-2017-ignition-index.notes: Public full text is deposited in the University of Córdoba repository. The graphical Table 2 was visually verified for all 18 exact taxa. The registry's earlier note claiming Thuja orientalis and Ligustrum vulgare were low-class mitigators was incorrect: they are classes 3 and 4. This UCO dataset is an independent molina-uco-tree lineage.

msu-e2948.name: Wildfire-resistant Landscape Plants for Michigan (Extension Bulletin E2948)
msu-e2948.scaleNotes: Binary wildfire-resistant list: Table 1 prints 241 rows (2 annuals, 27 groundcovers, 57 perennials, 86 shrubs, 60 trees, 9 vines) with hardiness zones and a Michigan-native flag. Verdict map: listed = recommend.
msu-e2948.notes: Michigan's only wildfire plant list. The current MSU PDF endpoint returned an Incapsula denial on 2026-08-25, so evidence links use the verified 2007 Internet Archive capture. Exact audit represents 226 source rows as 221 GBIF owners and holds 15 cultivar, hybrid-group, subspecies, or non-exact rows. Notable inclusions that collide with other lists — bird's nest spruce, English ivy, common boxwood — carry the usual recommend verdict here and surface as documented conflicts rather than being averaged away.

msu-montguide-mt200101ag.name: Fire-Resistant Plants for Montana Landscapes (MontGuide MT200101AG)
msu-montguide-mt200101ag.scaleNotes: Binary list of fire-resistant species adapted to Montana: 64 groundcover/herbaceous rows, 14 tree rows, and 18 shrub rows. Verdict map: listed = recommend.
msu-montguide-mt200101ag.notes: Tier 1 original regional expert curation by MSU Extension. The source acknowledges Bob Gough and Jason Lamb as the original authors and explains that some references rated whole genera while others named species. Its single Rosaceae-family row is preserved in the source archive but excluded from plant rating inputs because family is metadata, never a record rank or a cascading verdict.

nc-plant-toolbox.name: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — flammability ratings
nc-plant-toolbox.scaleNotes: Per-plant flammability tags — low / medium / high / extreme — on the Toolbox's plant pages and search facets. Verdict map: low = recommend, medium = mixed, high and extreme = avoid. Tier is deliberately omitted: the Toolbox does not document who assigned its flammability values, so rows count as corroboration only, never sole Tier 1 support. Rows for plants already rated by Bardon's 2005 Firewise Landscaping list resolve to bardon-2005 via the chain-to-root rule.
nc-plant-toolbox.notes: Facts extracted with attribution from the public search facets (240 rated plants, 2026-08-23); Toolbox photos are per-image licensed (many NC/ND) and are not reused. Exact-match audit 2026-08-25: 238 facet rows resolve to 217 existing GBIF owners; 10 rows use nine documented exact synonym/spelling/genus reconciliations, and two cultivar/hybrid labels are held. Three plants appear under both the high and extreme tags; both values are preserved. No undocumented Toolbox row can supply sole Tier 1 support.

ncsu-ag874.name: Fire-Resistant Landscaping in North Carolina (AG-874)
ncsu-ag874.publisher: NC State Extension (Kays, Fawcett, Query, Thompson-Welch, Bardon)
ncsu-ag874.scaleNotes: 202 North Carolina natives across three tables — 106 low, 61 medium, 35 high flammability — with growth-form groupings and habitat columns. Verdict map: low = recommend, medium = mixed, high = avoid. The successor to Bardon's 2005 Firewise Landscaping list (Bardon is a co-author): the 2005 "extreme" class was dropped, so former extreme species reappear here as high.
ncsu-ag874.notes: Rows whose class is unchanged from the 2005 list resolve to bardon-2005 (same nc-tree lineage, edition corroboration); rows where the class changed carry their own AG-874 evidence naming the delta. Not independent of bardon-2005 or of the NC Plant Toolbox rows that chain to it.

nfs-living-with-fire-nebraska.name: Living With Fire — A Homeowner's Guide, Eastern Nebraska Edition
nfs-living-with-fire-nebraska.scaleNotes: The exact instruction "Avoid juniper, mugo pine and arborvitae" maps the taxon-resolvable Juniperus genus and Pinus mugo species to avoid.
nfs-living-with-fire-nebraska.notes: The guide is adapted from the University of Nevada Living With Fire program. It has no plant table, but its Lean, Clean and Green Area tips contain a direct avoid sentence. Juniper and mugo pine support exact GBIF identities; arborvitae and the guide's other cedar/redcedar wording are held because the common names do not safely identify a single taxon. A currently indexed Western Nebraska companion timed out during retrieval, so no facts were reconstructed from its search result. Eastern-edition PDF SHA-256: 495902d0ae6adfc2f17ec8da69233f0535e5bf795afa29aed0c42af6b3248c90.

nord-green-1977-psw124.name: Low-volume and slow-burning vegetation for planting on clearings in California chaparral
nord-green-1977-psw124.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Pacific Southwest Forest and Range Experiment Station
nord-green-1977-psw124.scaleNotes: Table 2 recommends named grasses for California fuelbreak sites. Tables 3 and 4 classify shrub field performance as Good, Fair, or Poor for southern California brushland clearings; Table 5 separately lists 22 shrub taxa not considered suitable, with reasons that include establishment, adaptation, fuel volume, morphology, and flammability.
nord-green-1977-psw124.notes: Performance and suitability are preserved as source placement evidence. Poor and unsuitable rows are recorded as not-rated rather than as avoid evidence because many failures concern establishment or site adaptation rather than intrinsic flammability. Capture SHA-256: bea653b39eb3e133339e7d18f5ceac68d28d760fb62a8be4bb4842e7154e9e39.

nrcs-tn66-fuel-breaks-2016.name: Fuel Breaks to Reduce Large Wildfire Impacts in Sagebrush Ecosystems (Plant Materials Technical Note 66)
nrcs-tn66-fuel-breaks-2016.publisher: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Boise, Idaho
nrcs-tn66-fuel-breaks-2016.scaleNotes: Appendix B is a 12-row table headed “Common plant material options for greenstrips.” Listed = recommend only within the recorded greenstrip placement; the rows are not unconditional home-landscape recommendations. The crested-wheatgrass row names two alternative species and therefore resolves to two exact GBIF evidence owners.
nrcs-tn66-fuel-breaks-2016.notes: Tier 1 agency synthesis with an explicit operational selection framework. The note says greenstrip materials should be selected primarily for adaptation and persistence, and that establishment and maintenance can include site preparation, grazing deferment, grazing, mowing, or herbicide. osfm-oregon-fire-resistant-plants.scaleNotes: Presence as one of six results under the page's “Which Fire-Resistant Plant Are You?” quiz. The agency page points readers to OSU's PNW 590 guide, so these rows are Tier 2 corroboration in the pnw590-tree, not independent votes.

osu-b921.name: Firewise Landscaping (OSU Extension Bulletin 921)
osu-b921.publisher: Ohio State University Extension (Sydnor, Steward, Kloss / Ohio DNR Division of Forestry)

osu-em-9103.name: Fire-resistant Landscape Plants for the Willamette Valley (EM 9103)
osu-em-9103.scaleNotes: Binary recommendation by presence among the publication's 178 individual groundcover, perennial, shrub/woody-vine, and tree profiles. Verdict map: profiled as fire-resistant = recommend.
osu-em-9103.notes: OSU's Willamette Valley companion to PNW 590. The introduction says the guide highlights fire-resistant plants that thrive under Willamette Valley growing conditions and points readers to PNW 590 for more information, so both sources remain one pnw590-tree lineage vote. The legacy OSU and registry PDF endpoints returned 403 on 2026-08-25; the captured complete OSU publication is hosted by Canby Fire District. osu-plant-profile-galleries.name: Fire-resistant plant profile galleries
osu-plant-profile-galleries.scaleNotes: Binary recommendation by presence in one of five galleries whose headings direct readers to choose the profiled plants for a fire-resistant landscape. Verdict map: profiled = recommend.
osu-plant-profile-galleries.notes: Web presentation of the 2023 PNW 590 list, with descriptive profiles and printed USDA zones. The gallery pages explicitly point to PNW 590 for complete details, so both sources remain one pnw590-tree lineage vote. Exact reconciliation represents 146 printed taxon alternatives from 155 profiles on 145 GBIF owners. Thirteen cultivar-specific, hybrid-group, or non-exact profiles are held; the shrub and tree galleries' two Serviceberry profiles remain separate evidence rows on the shared Amelanchier owner.

ozbreed-fire-retardant-plants.name: Fire Retardant Plants: Literature Review and Plant List
ozbreed-fire-retardant-plants.scaleNotes: List 1 contains plants backed by scientific evidence or longstanding use as fire breaks; List 2 contains Ozbreed plants whose genus and species appear regularly on multiple fire-retardant lists; List 3 contains selections that appear on fewer lists or require extra management. Lists 1 and 2 map to recommend; the explicitly management-dependent List 3 maps to mixed.
ozbreed-fire-retardant-plants.notes: Twenty unique, taxonomically resolvable genus/species identities were admitted. Cultivars were collapsed only to the species explicitly printed beside them; cultivar-only Rhododendron and Gazania hybrids, an unspecified Westringia cultivar, and Dianella hybrid were held rather than widened to an inferred species. The five comparison rows in the CSIRO sample table are not recommendations and are already represented by primary-study measurements in FLAMITS. pnw-590.name: Fire-Resistant Plants for Home Landscapes (PNW 590)
pnw-590.publisher: OSU + WSU + University of Idaho Extension (joint PNW series)
pnw-590.scaleNotes: Binary recommend (presence on list). Carries USDA zone ranges per plant.
pnw-590.notes: Root of the largest US derivation tree. Joint publication of three land-grant universities; the most-mirrored fire plant document in the West.

radtke-1983-psw-gtr-067.name: Living More Safely in the Chaparral-Urban Interface
radtke-1983-psw-gtr-067.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Pacific Southwest Forest and Range Experiment Station (Klaus W. H. Radtke)
radtke-1983-psw-gtr-067.scaleNotes: Table 5 assigns 20 low-growing landscape entries a fire-retardance class based on fuel volume, inherent plant flammability, and ease of fire spread. High and generally high map to recommend; medium, medium to high, and low to medium map to mixed; low maps to avoid. The collective ice-plants row explicitly names Carpobrotus, Delosperma, and Drosanthemum, so it produces three genus-level rows. The 2004 revision republishes a nine-entry subset without changing these classes.
radtke-1983-psw-gtr-067.notes: The report says its table is a general guide for southern California rather than a substitute for site advice. Its ratings are kept in the existing la-arboretum-tree because Radtke cites that plant-selection lineage and acts as a popularizer rather than a new independent taxon trial. Modern taxon queries correct obvious historical spellings only where the report supplies an unambiguous scientific identity; verbatim table labels remain in verdictRaw. scfc-fire-smart-plant-list.name: Landscaping Can Be Attractive & FIREWISE (Fire Smart Plant List for SC)
scfc-fire-smart-plant-list.scaleNotes: The source's HIGHLY Flammable Plants section maps to avoid. Its LESS Flammable Plants with some fire resistance section maps to recommend.
scfc-fire-smart-plant-list.notes: The two-page brochure was created in January 2005 and later re-hosted by SCFC. It supplies common names only and cites no underlying list or method. Ingestion therefore remains at genus rank: 72 unique source labels have a conservative genus identity, collapsing to 63 exact accepted-GBIF evidence owners. Arborvitae, pine straw, and Cleyera are held because the labels do not support a single safe genus mapping; the repeated Spirea bullet is represented once. No species were inferred from common names. Tier remains unset and lineage unknown. Official PDF SHA-256: e75db5c74551ea0977b0fb08cfd258b40328f29e7c4b4586cebdcb38bd3a5f57.

sdsu-protecting-home-landscape.name: Protecting Your Home and Landscape Against Wildfires
sdsu-protecting-home-landscape.scaleNotes: The sentence naming common flammable trees maps Juniperus, Pinus, Abies, and Picea genus rows to avoid. The adjacent text discourages conifers in the immediate and intermediate Home Ignition Zones.
sdsu-protecting-home-landscape.notes: The page supplies four safe genus identities and no separate low-flammability taxon list. Its references include South Dakota Wildland Fire, NFPA, USDA Black Hills National Forest, CSU, and USU, but the genus sentence has no cell-level provenance or method, so lineage remains unknown. Official HTML SHA-256: f9a7b9901ef1b6e4301e75adb59905e01ed641cbf5264f0e0be41fba510c9d63.

shan-2003-leaf-fire-ranking.name: Ordering and sorting of fire resistance of tree leaves
shan-2003-leaf-fire-ranking.publisher: Scientia Silvae Sinicae (Shan, Hu, Shu, Xu)
shan-2003-leaf-fire-ranking.scaleNotes: The paper ranks 55 litter-leaf taxa after factor analysis of moisture, ignition point, ash, heat of combustion, and extractives. Only the authors' explicitly named ten best and ten worst taxa are verdict-bearing: best = recommend and worst = avoid. Uninterpreted middle rankings and clusters are not mapped.

Nineteen of the twenty author-classified source taxa resolve exactly through GBIF into eighteen accepted records; the two larches share one accepted concept. Ledum palustre var. dilatatum is excluded because GBIF resolves the printed name only to genus. The other 35 measured taxa remain unmapped rather than receiving inferred verdicts.

souza-2024-promptus-thermal.name: Thermal analysis of low-flammability plants for green barriers against forest fires
souza-2024-promptus-thermal.publisher: Promptus, Revista Técnico-Científica do CBMDF (Souza, Vale & Chaves)
souza-2024-promptus-thermal.scaleNotes: The authors explicitly retain three low-flammability classes and the Echinolaena high-flammability comparator after combustion, TGA, and DSC tests. All four exact taxa are represented. The authors and 2013-14 collection program overlap Souza and Vale 2019; the new combustion/TGA measurements enrich the same unb-cbmdf-tree vote rather than creating a second lineage.

souza-vale-2019-cerrado-df.publisher: Ciência Florestal (Souza & Vale; Universidade de Brasília and CBMDF)
souza-vale-2019-cerrado-df.scaleNotes: The authors explicitly classify three repeatedly preserved taxa as low flammability and Echinolaena inflexa as the high-flammability comparator. souza-vale-2019-cerrado-df.notes: Complete Portuguese full text and an English abstract are openly published by UFSM. Seven burned areas totaling about 40 ha were walked within four days of fire; multiple preserved individuals were documented beside consumed vegetation, followed by leaf physical-property analysis. Verdict map: named-flammable = avoid, works-well = recommend. Thirteen taxa, resolved from common names with the resolution recorded on each row.

unr-compilation-good-plant-choices.name: A Compilation of Good Plant Choices for Nevada's High Fire Hazard Areas (SP-05-16)

unr-compilation-good-plant-choices.notes: Tier 2 corroboration only. unr-fs-97-36-greenstrips.name: Greenstrips: Another Tool to Manage Wildfire (Fact Sheet 97-36)

Fourteen rows fit the current taxon-rank schema; Poa canbyi is held out because its exact GBIF match resolves to a subspecies rank the schema cannot represent.
unr-fs-97-36-greenstrips.notes: Tier 1 extension curation with stated selection requirements: adaptation, establishment amid annual weeds, separated growth, low mature height, low fuel production, long green period, post-burn survival, and grazing tolerance. The note says greenstrips should be grazed or mown frequently enough to reduce fuel buildup. Same greenstrip-tree lineage as BLM, NRCS, and the cited 1986 University of Nevada fact sheet.

usfs-feis.name: Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)
usfs-feis.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Missoula Fire Sciences Laboratory
usfs-feis.scaleNotes: Narrative species reviews; no single rating scale.
usfs-feis.notes: Public-domain federal fire-ecology syntheses, one review per taxon, each citing the primary literature it summarizes. Registered 2026-08-24 as the approved corroborator and context source for genus/species prose (genus-notes): it synthesizes other people's measurements and observations, so it counts as corroboration and citation context, NEVER as an independent Tier 1 line of evidence, and it never votes in a derivation.

usu-firewise-plants-utah.name: Firewise Plants for Utah Landscapes (NR/FF/002)
usu-firewise-plants-utah.scaleNotes: Binary list of 83 plants or plant groups that the source says can be firewise when properly placed and maintained. Verdict map: listed = recommend. Asterisks identify plants that may become weedy; they do not change the source's firewise verdict.
usu-firewise-plants-utah.notes: Tier 1 expert curation by Michael Kuhns. Utah FFSL's 2007 Firewise Landscaping for Utah book was authored by Kuhns and Barbara Daniels and expands this fact sheet, so both publications belong to the single usu-kuhns lineage and never count as independent votes.

ut-sp685.name: Landscaping Guidelines to Protect Your Home from Wildfire (SP685)
ut-sp685.scaleNotes: Binary Firewise plant tables (78 taxa). Verdict map: listed = recommend.
ut-sp685.notes: A carrier, not an independent rater: SP685's plant tables are verbatim copies of Virginia Firescapes 430-300 rows (confirmed by row-text comparison; 430-300 is cited in its references), so rows landing on records with va-firescapes evidence resolve to that root. A handful of Tennessee-specific additions (Chinese fringetree, cornelian cherry, rabbiteye blueberry, Thunberg spirea) stay as SP685's own Tier 2 rows.

utah-ffsl-firewise-landscaping.name: Firewise Landscaping for Utah (2007)
utah-ffsl-firewise-landscaping.publisher: Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands / Utah State University Extension Forestry
utah-ffsl-firewise-landscaping.scaleNotes: The book expands Michael Kuhns's 1998/2005 USU Firewise Plants for Utah Landscapes fact sheet and is the same evidence lineage. Its recommend tables are not duplicated. The separately printed PLANTS TO AVOID passage supplies four tree-genus pyrophyte rows and one cheatgrass row.
utah-ffsl-firewise-landscaping.notes: The live FFSL file is gone; the recovered 40-page PDF and layout-preserving text are archived locally. Five avoid rows are ingested from page 15. The recommend tables remain represented by the 2005 USU root and never count as a second independent vote. No images were fetched.

uts-2023-street-trees.name: Shoot flammability patterns in native and exotic street tree species at the WUI of eastern Australia
uts-2023-street-trees.publisher: Fire (Huber-Smith, Morley, Krix, Murray et al.; University of Technology Sydney)
uts-2023-street-trees.region: Central Coast, New South Wales, Australia
uts-2023-street-trees.scaleNotes: The paper finds that rankings across time-to-flame, flame duration, number of flaming events, and flame temperature are not concordant. Verdict map: the sole taxon the authors identify across attributes as a potential low-flammability street-tree candidate = recommend; every other measured taxon = mixed. No per-attribute extreme is promoted to an overall verdict.
uts-2023-street-trees.notes: Public full text is available from the UTS repository and the OA publisher. All ten species are represented. Krix and Murray recur across the UTS program, so this is one uts-murray-tree vote. The burner design follows the Jaureguiberry/Wyse method, but there is no author or dataset overlap with the Lincoln papers; method adoption alone does not merge those lineages.

uw-barnyards-firewise-2005.name: Firewise Landscaping
uw-barnyards-firewise-2005.publisher: University of Wyoming Extension, Barnyards & Backyards (Jody Walker, USDA NRCS)
uw-barnyards-firewise-2005.scaleNotes: The article explicitly separates examples of fire-prone plants from examples of fire-resistant plants and plants for a Firewise landscape. Fire-prone maps to avoid; fire-resistant and Firewise examples map to recommend.
uw-barnyards-firewise-2005.notes: Ten examples have unambiguous species or genus identities. “Most conifers,” cottonwood, aspens, mahogany, mountain maple, succulents, herbaceous species, wildflowers, and groundcovers were held because the printed common or group name does not define one exact taxon. Repeated examples were represented once. PDF SHA-256: 77cd64f5ff73ce54877f0892b7d14a6498008fcf36d5b524321b358f3d31ba77.

va-firescapes.name: Virginia Firescapes — Firewise Landscaping for Woodland Homes (430-300)
va-firescapes.publisher: Virginia Cooperative Extension / Virginia Tech (Appleton, Frenzel, Hillegass, Lyons, Steward — Virginia Firewise Landscaping Task Force)
va-firescapes.scaleNotes: Three-point flammability rating (H / M / L, "more or less forest fire-prone") across six tables of deciduous and evergreen trees and shrubs, groundcovers, and vines. Verdict map: L = recommend, M = mixed, H = avoid. Every evergreen tree and shrub in the list is rated H.
va-firescapes.notes: Produced by the Virginia Firewise Landscaping Task Force (Virginia Tech, Virginia Department of Forestry, soil and water district, and Larry Steward). Steward also rated the Fire Performance Plant Selector and co-authored OSU B921, so the three lists share a rater and are not fully independent of one another. Nativity column marks Virginia natives; a blank cell means not marked native, not a verdict. Clematis virginiana's rating cell is blank in the printed source (verified against the page image) and is recorded as not-rated. The Ilex x 'Nellie R. Stevens' cultivar row is taxonomy-held because GBIF has no exact cultivar match; it is not broadened to the genus or a parent hybrid.

valette-1990.name: Inflammabilités des espèces forestières méditerranéennes (Valette 1990)
valette-1990.publisher: INRA Station de Sylviculture méditerranéenne, Avignon (Revue Forestière Française XLII)
valette-1990.scaleNotes: Epiradiator inflammability testing (ignition frequency x mean ignition delay) producing monthly inflammability notes 0-5 for 32 Mediterranean species across May-April — 0 peu inflammable through 5 extrêmement inflammable. Verdict map (recorded judgment): the July-September fire-season maximum note drives the verdict — 0-2 recommend, 3 mixed, 4-5 avoid — with the full monthly row preserved as a claim and the original French class term quoted.
valette-1990.notes: The French laboratory root: INRA Avignon's standard inflammability protocol, the evidence base behind Provence garden guidance and the reference method across the western Mediterranean. First non-English source in the corpus under the all-English extraction policy. Notable rows: rosemary peaks at 3 (inflammable), holm oak and chestnut at 5, the eucalypts at 5 year-round, cypress at 2-3.

valparaiso-2021-leaf-thermal-chemical.name: Leaf thermal and chemical properties as natural drivers of plant flammability
valparaiso-2021-leaf-thermal-chemical.region: Peñuelas Lake National Reserve, Valparaíso, Chile
valparaiso-2021-leaf-thermal-chemical.scaleNotes: Table 2 applies Valette's 0-5 live-leaf flammability index. Verdict map: 0-1 = recommend; 2-3 = mixed; 4-5 = avoid. Ignition frequency and mean ignition time are retained per species.
valparaiso-2021-leaf-thermal-chemical.notes: Complete CC-BY full text and Table 2 are public. All five exact taxa are represented. Guerrero/UTFSM, the Peñuelas study site, and the species panel overlap the 2020 thermochemistry paper, so both remain one guerrero-utfsm-tree vote despite the new epiradiator measurements.

wa-dnr-eastern-wa.name: Fire-Resistant Plants for Eastern Washington
wa-dnr-eastern-wa.publisher: Washington State Department of Natural Resources
wa-dnr-eastern-wa.notes: Master Gardener compilation. Its own acknowledgments state it "lists only fire-resistant plants that are in other Firewise documents" and that no empirical research was performed. Lineage unknown but likely overlaps the PNW 590 tree; WA DNR separately hosts PNW 590 (2006) verbatim. Counts as corroboration, never as an independent Tier 1 line of evidence.

wdnr-uwex.name: Firewise Landscaping — A Guide to Protecting Your Home from Wildfire
wdnr-uwex.scaleNotes: Binary-recommend guide: named "Firewise Plant" profiles plus a table of suggested firewise plants also suitable for shoreland buffers. Verdict map: listed = recommend. The archived extract yields 22 verifiable taxa (7 sidebar profiles + 15 wet-habitat table species).
wdnr-uwex.notes: Minnesota DNR defers to this Wisconsin guide, so its rows also serve the Minnesota audience. Small corroborator; several profile species already carry stronger evidence in the corpus.

white-etal-2002-cone-update.name: Cone calorimeter testing of vegetation — an update
white-etal-2002-cone-update.publisher: USDA Forest Service (White, Weise, Mackes & Dibble)
white-etal-2002-cone-update.region: Colorado, California, and northeastern United States
white-etal-2002-cone-update.scaleNotes: The conclusion explicitly names high- and low-relative-flammability taxa. Verdict map: author-named high = avoid; author-named low = recommend; other exactly identified and measured Colorado taxa = mixed. Table 4 green-sample PHRR is preserved as score and dry-sample EHOC is preserved in each claim.
white-etal-2002-cone-update.notes: Complete public full text is hosted by USDA Forest Service. Fourteen exact Colorado taxa were ingested; Artemisia sp. was excluded because it is only identified to genus. The California and Northeast datasets are excluded from this extraction because later papers in the same USFS-FPL cone-calorimeter program report them. White/Dibble/Weise author and method overlap means all such rows remain one usfs-fpl-cone-tree vote.

wildlife-qld-fire-resistant-natives.name: Protect your home and wildlife — top fire-resistant native plants for Queensland backyards
wildlife-qld-fire-resistant-natives.scaleNotes: The article explicitly presents three named native species as fire-resistant choices for Queensland backyards and separately describes buffel grass as highly combustible and able to carry fire rapidly. The three positive statements map to recommend and the buffel-grass warning maps to avoid.
wildlife-qld-fire-resistant-natives.notes: Four exact GBIF species owners were admitted: three existing records were enriched and one was created. The page links Paten Park Native Nursery only under "Further information and to buy plants" and does not attribute its claims, so the evidence lineage remains unknown rather than inferred. Live HTML SHA-256 fb6899d40e0d648f713d5dd77b7fb2b46f1b4a0ce43d38806965ff7ec92c8fd3; WordPress API JSON SHA-256 2fac7c6013b15351c905630f5287d1879ddbaba3e9ca2f94f725eaf30ec2220a.

wyse-2016-nz-60-species.name: A quantitative assessment of shoot flammability for 60 tree and shrub species
wyse-2016-nz-60-species.publisher: International Journal of Wildland Fire (Wyse, Perry, O'Connell, Holland, Wright, Hosted, Whitelock, Geary, Maurin, Curran)
wyse-2016-nz-60-species.scaleNotes: Figure 2 assigns all 60 tested species to k-means clusters on the first principal-component axis: low, low/moderate, moderate, moderate/high, high, or very high. Verdict map: low and low/moderate = recommend; moderate and moderate/high = mixed; high and very high = avoid. The map is applied once for this source and does not infer thresholds from plotted positions.
wyse-2016-nz-60-species.notes: Direct shoot-flammability evidence from the Lincoln University program. Freshly collected shoots were air-dried for 24 hours before testing. This is the same lincoln-nz-tree as later Cui/Curran papers and the FENZ directory, so it is one lineage vote. The full article is publicly available from the Lincoln University Research Archive; DOI 10.1071/WF15047.

yavapai-34.name: Fire-Resistant and Fire-Prone Plants Common to Yavapai County (Bulletin 34)
yavapai-34.publisher: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension, Yavapai County
yavapai-34.scaleNotes: The bulletin has two named lists. Its 150 usable Fire-Resistant Plants entries map to recommend, and its 50 usable Fire-Prone Plants entries map to avoid. The bulletin says resistant plants are not fireproof and require irrigation and maintenance; fire-prone plants may ignite readily and burn intensely.
yavapai-34.notes: Ingested every usable scientific entry in the two tables. Entries printed at genus rank remain genus records, including four labels that an earlier parser draft had silently widened to species. "Arborvitae — Thuja, Platycladus" is represented by its two explicitly printed genera. The invalid scientific cell "Pinion" and ten informal, family-level, or taxon-free entries were held rather than inferred from their common names. Obvious extraction damage and botanical spelling errors were repaired only when the printed identity was unambiguous; accepted-name reconciliation required exact GBIF matches. The bulletin states no methods or citations, so its tier is left unset and lineage remains unknown. Official PDF SHA-256: 38b1bce8d164c27b5fb23d3bad51a23d92dc69dc0f24a69e899d72a2536b382a.
